commits.message:
Allow one tick between the process and main-thread CPU totals

The kernel rounds a thread's CPU time and its process's total to clock ticks separately, so over a 300 ms spin the process total can read one tick below the main thread's. CI shard 1 on a138ba907 failed exactly that way: 0.8306 against 0.8638 cores, one 10 ms tick over 0.301 s. The test now allows one tick of slack.

Refs #871

Key the recent tx id index so ground ids cannot share one probe chain

The recent-id ring placed each id at the cell its own first four bytes named. A submitter can grind tx ids that share those bits and get them admitted, piling them into one probe chain that every duplicate check on the main thread then walks; the ring's own model test, whose ids share five prefixes, ran 200 s locally and timed out in CI at 783 s. The home cell now comes from SHA-256 over a per-process secret and the id, stored per slot so growth and deletion never hash again.

Tests: a new case remembers 40,000 ids sharing their first eight bytes within 15 s. It timed out at 15 s on the unkeyed ring and takes 147 ms keyed. The model test compares fields directly, with one assertion per checkpoint, and runs in 3 s instead of 200 s.

Refs #874

Delete the admission writer's obsolete module-size exception

The in-memory writer rewrite left admission-writer.make-admission-writer-with-options.ts at 492 lines, inside the 500-line default, and the size guard refuses an exception a file no longer needs.

Repoint the two doc citations of the deleted admission module

#872 removed txAdmissions.admit-without-byte-quota.ts. The F3 decision memo now links to the file at the commit it was read against, and the ingress design names the removed module in the past tense.

Point the load harness test and the M2 bench at the in-memory admission writer

Since /submit answers from memory, the harness stack test counted queued rows before the writer had committed the last group; it now waits for the writer first. The M2 bench stubbed the removed admitReserved method; its writer stub now implements lookup and admit, and the SqlClient stub for the removed direct-admission fallback is gone.

Refs #871 #874

Retry admission writes through database outages instead of dropping the txs

The writer retried only serialization failures, deadlocks, lock timeouts, cancelled statements and lost connections. A full disk (53100), an out-of-memory server (53200), an I/O error (58030) or a server left read-only by a failover (25006) counted as a fault of the row, so the batch split and every acknowledged tx was dropped one by one as poisoned. These outages fail every row alike; retried, they show as the writer stall (503 and not ready) and clear once the database recovers.

Test: the pipeline retry case now runs once per code. Red before the fix: expected { code: '53100', attempts: 1 } to deeply equal { code: '53100', attempts: 3 }.

Refs #874

Say that a duplicate still answers 200 while the admission backlog is full

The backlog paragraph in PUBLIC_HTTP.md still said a full backlog refused a resubmitted duplicate. Since the ack moved into memory, the duplicate lookup runs before any backlog reservation, so a duplicate answers 200 whatever the backlog holds.

Acknowledge /submit from memory with a bounded pending set (#874)

/submit and /peer/txs waited for the admission row's commit before
answering, so every request held an HTTP slot through a Postgres round trip
and a slow database stalled the whole ingress. Per the D9 ruling the node
now answers once the checked transaction is in the admission writer's
in-memory pending set, with the backlog gauges reserved before the 202, and
the row follows by per-lane group commit.

- Duplicates are answered from the pending set, then from a bounded cache of
  recently written native ids (a typed-array ring, 1M ids), with no database
  read. A cache entry stops answering once its row may have been pruned
  (ADMISSION_TERMINAL_RETENTION_MS), so a late resubmission is admitted and
  validated again as before. Peer rows are not cached: the tx-queue
  processor deletes a peer row whose inputs it has not seen, and the next
  offer must reach the database again.
- A same-id variant that only the database holds is resolved after the ack:
  the stored version stays and a counter records it.
- Transient write failures retry with backoff and keep the txs pending;
  other failures split the batch and write row by row; a row that still
  fails is dropped with a counter and an error log, so it cannot block its
  shard.
- When the oldest pending tx has waited longer than 30 s, /submit and
  /peer/txs answer 503 and /readyz reports admission_writer_stalled; both
  clear by themselves once writes succeed.
- A graceful stop flushes for at most 10 s, then counts and logs the ids it
  could not write. The flush is made interruptible: finalizers run
  uninterruptibly, so without it the timeout could not end the wait and a
  stop with Postgres stalled would hang.
- /tx-status reports pending txs as queued and /peer/inventory treats them
  as known.

Visible changes the existing tests now pin: a duplicate answered from
memory reports the status the node wrote (/tx-status has the verdict) and
no longer bumps request_count; a duplicate still answers 200 while the
backlog is full; a peer re-offer of a tx that is already written counts as
admitted, since only pending peer txs are known in memory. The peer test
helper flushes the writer before it drains the queue. The writer's readiness
check lives in its own module so readiness.ts stays under the size limit.

The Postgres-backed tests hold ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on tx_admissions from
another connection: /submit still answers 202, /tx-status answers queued and
duplicates answer 200 within the lock; a capped writer fills, stalls,
answers 503 and recovers when the lock is released; a 31-byte id that the
table's CHECK refuses is dropped while its batch is written; a stop writes
every pending tx, and a stop under the lock ends within its bound (red
without the interruptible flush: the test timed out). A recent id older
than its age bound stops answering (red with the bound removed). The
recent-id ring is checked against a reference model through growth and
eviction with ids that share probe chains.

PUBLIC_HTTP.md and the docs-site API page now say that 202 means accepted,
not stored, and that a crash can lose acknowledged transactions.

Record the measured submit check and handler costs in the ingress design

The decode-once check measures 0.075, 0.12 and 0.33 ms for the 1/2, 4/4 and 16/16 shapes, well under the stale-build figures the plan carried. Today's whole /submit handler costs 475-600 us of main thread per request, so one thread saturates near 2,000 req/s and the lean handler (#881) is required for 5,000 TPS. The plan now names its tracking issue instead of saying it has no tickets.

Serve the public node only on a Unix socket behind its TLS ingress

The public profiles used to open a TLS listener on TCP in the node, with an
optional nginx in front on a fixed Docker subnet that the node trusted by
address. Every public request paid TLS in the node, nginx rate limited submit
and read routes ahead of the node's own limiter, and nginx cut the node's
connections at 100 requests each.

The node now serves plain HTTP only on HTTP_SOCKET_PATH on the public
profiles and opens no TCP listener; TLS ends at nginx. The socket's
directory must grant other users no access, the socket is made 0660, and a
socket a killed node left behind is replaced so a restart needs no manual
cleanup. On the socket the node takes each client from x-midgard-client-ip,
which nginx sets to the connecting address. The stack always runs the
ingress: a socket directory of mode 0700 in the run directory is mounted
into the node and the ingress only, both run as the host user, and the
ingress sits on a network of its own with no TCP route to the node.

nginx keeps upstream connections alive to the socket (the node no longer
caps requests per socket there), drops limit_req from submit and read
routes, keeps a per-address connection cap and the liveness/admin rate
zone, caps /submit and /tx/evaluate bodies at SUBMIT_HTTP_BODY_MAX_BYTES,
and answers its own refusals as JSON with Retry-After and the node's error
codes.

HTTP_TRUSTED_PROXY_PEERS, for a node on TCP, now takes up to 64 IPv4 or
IPv6 addresses or ranges (at least /8 and /24, no host bits) so a cloud load
balancer's published ranges fit; it is refused together with
HTTP_SOCKET_PATH. The listener transport moves out of listen-public-http.ts
into listen-http-transport.ts to keep that file under the line limit.

Test gate: public-ingress.test.mjs renders the config and serves it with a
real nginx in front of a stub node on a socket. It fails if a request rate
returns to submit or read routes (1,000 r/s from one client must all reach
the node), if the body cap drifts from the node's limit, or if nginx
forwards the client's own x-midgard-client-ip; no existing test ran nginx.
The listener tests fail if the public profile opens TCP, accepts a socket
directory others can enter, leaves the socket world-writable, or cannot
start over a stale socket; they extend the existing listen-public-http and
rate-limit suites. CI runs the ingress test next to the operator compose
derivation test.

Refs #879

Delete admission payloads at the terminal mark and retire old terminal rows (#875)

Nothing reads tx_admission_payloads after an admission's verdict:
acceptance copies the bytes into the mempool table, peer sharing reads
that copy, and the duplicate check compares the full hash on the
admission row since #872. The payload still sat there forever, and every
terminal admission row stayed too, so the primary key grew with every
transaction (3.6M rows an hour at 1,000 TPS).

Mark-accepted and mark-rejected now delete the payload row in the same
transaction, and the accepted path checks the deleted count with the
others. Migration 35 drops the payloads of rows already terminal and adds
a partial (terminal_at, tx_id) index.

A new retention fiber deletes accepted and rejected rows older than
ADMISSION_TERMINAL_RETENTION_MS (default one hour, 0 keeps them) in
batches of 5,000, up to 60 batches a minute. It keeps a row while
mempool or processed_mempool holds its tx, because the mempool page
order, replay order and peer catch-up read its arrival_seq, and while
tx_rejections holds it, because a re-admitted tx rejected with another
code would fail the exactly-once rejection insert and stall its batch.
Candidates are taken with SKIP LOCKED, so the sweep never waits on a
lock, and a keyset cursor carried across sweeps (kept as Postgres text so
it keeps microseconds) walks past rows that must stay. /tx-status never
reads a terminal admission row, so deleting one changes no answer.

Tests: the rejection and acceptance journal tests now check that no
payload is left after the mark, that an exact resubmission is still a
duplicate and that the same id with other witnesses still answers 409;
removing the payload delete from mark-rejected fails the first with
"expected [ ...(8) ] to deeply equal []". A new Postgres-backed retention
test checks which rows go and which stay, and that a walk over held rows
at one timestamp still reaches the deletable rows behind them.

Add the submit ingress load harness, drain stub and M2 bench (#871)

Phase P0 of the public submit ingress design needs a baseline of /submit apart from block production. scripts/submit-ingress-load.mjs builds a corpus of valid txs (each spending its own genesis output) plus a junk mix (bad CBOR, bad signature, low fee, missing input, double spend), offers it one tx per request at a fixed open-loop rate, mostly on new connections, from many client addresses (the trusted-proxy header straight to the node, or loopback source addresses through an edge on the host network), and writes a report: admitted rate, outcome mix overall and per kind, latency quantiles, admission rows/s and Postgres write rates, and the node's main-thread and process CPU from /proc. The drain stub marks queued admissions terminal at a set rate under E_LOAD_DRAIN_STUB, so ingress is measured without validation or blocks.

The corpus test runs every request through the real submit check, Phase A and Phase B against the corpus genesis and requires each kind to land where the manifest says: valid accepted, bad CBOR refused at ingress, bad signature and low fee at Phase A, missing input and double spend at Phase B. The stack test drives the client against the production /submit route and admission writer in process, then empties the queue with the drain stub. The l2-peer-node helper takes an optional ingress policy so that test can turn the rate limits off.

bench:submit-main-thread is M2: main-thread CPU per /submit with the admission writer stubbed and the client in a child process.

Refs #871

Drop the unknown-length submit holder from the peer permit test

The submit route now answers a body with no declared length with 411 before it takes a permit (#878), so a holder of unknown length can no longer fill the submit byte budget and the row waited for a pool that never filled. The count-based holder still proves submit users cannot starve /peer/txs.

Refs #878

Refuse at once when the admission writer is full and group-commit its batches (#873)

The writer took a semaphore slot per request, so a full writer parked every
further request (and its body) on a wait with no byte bound, and each batch
waited out a deadline even when the database was idle. Admission commits
also paid a synchronous WAL flush per batch, and readiness failed at a
fixed 10,000 rows however large the backlog bound was.

The writer now counts rows and bytes across every stage and refuses with
AdmissionWriterFullError the moment either bound (queue capacity, 64 MiB)
would be exceeded; /submit and /peer/txs answer 503 and the gauge treats
the refusal as proof nothing was inserted. Each shard's collector waits
for its persister to be free and then takes everything queued, up to 256
rows, with no clock: a lone request is written immediately and a busy
database gets ever larger batches. Admission batches run with
SET LOCAL synchronous_commit = off (owner ruling 2026-11-06; a lost tail
after a crash is a dropped acknowledged submission, not a safety fault).
Rows are still inserted in tx-id order so concurrent batches lock in one
order, but arrival_seq is now drawn in request order, so FIFO claiming
holds across a group-committed batch.

Readiness reports queue_depth_exceeded once the backlog passes 95 % of
MAX_DURABLE_ADMISSION_BACKLOG; READINESS_MAX_DURABLE_ADMISSION_BACKLOG
is no longer read.

Limit public submissions with fixed-memory hashed buckets per client and prefix

The public rate limiter kept one Map entry per client address, capped at HTTP_PEER_MAX_ENTRIES and tied to a config-time idle-window check. A flood of distinct addresses filled the table and refused every new client, and an IPv6 subscriber could claim a fresh key per /64.

Public classes now use two rows of 2^18 hashed cells (Float32 tokens, Uint32 whole-second refill stamps, Uint16 in-flight counts), keyed by a per-process secret. Memory is fixed however many clients arrive. A client is an IPv4 address or an IPv6 /56 (IPv4-mapped IPv6 counts as IPv4); writes also pass a prefix tier on the /24 or /48. Submissions default to 20 tx/s per client with burst 100 and 200 tx/s (burst 1,000) per prefix, charged one token per transaction, with no global write cap. Health, admin and peer keep a small exact table of 8,192 entries that evicts the least recently used idle entry instead of refusing. HTTP_PEER_MAX_ENTRIES, httpPublicKeysPerIdleWindow and the idle-window config check are gone, and HTTP_RATE_LIMIT_WRITE now takes client then prefix pairs.

Tests: listen-http-rate-buckets.test.ts drives the ingress with a fake clock. It fails if the limiter keeps per-client state (1,000,000 distinct clients must leave the exhausted client refused, with bounded heap growth), if a /48 can spread over its /56s past the prefix rate, if refill stamps wrap at 2^32 ms, or if in-flight slots are not held per client. No existing test covered hashed state, prefix tiers or the clock wrap; the old table-capacity tests were replaced, not extended, because the behavior they pinned is removed.
